article.headline: Browser-Based MMD Animation Editor Built on Three.js
article.lede: The official Three.js account highlighted Reze Studio, a web-based 3D animation tool that runs entirely in a browser. The screenshot reveals a fully featured bone hierarchy editor playing back a MikuMikuDance motion file at 60 frames per second. It is a demonstration of how far WebGL tooling has come in replicating desktop-class animation workflows.
article.body:
Reze Studio, currently at version 0.10 and accessible at reze.studio, displays a humanoid rig with **147 bones** organized into named chains — upper body, arms, hands, and lower body — alongside a morph targets panel for facial and mesh deformation. The animation being played is a `.vmd` file (the native motion format of *MikuMikuDance*, a long-running free animation program used heavily in Japanese fan communities). The timeline reads frame 1086 of 2889, with interpolation curves — linear, ease-in, ease-out — controllable per bone channel, which is the same granularity offered by professional desktop tools.

The fact that this runs in a browser owes almost everything to **Three.js**, the open-source JavaScript library that wraps WebGL's low-level graphics API into a usable scene graph. Three.js (GitHub: `mrdoob/three.js`) has shipped an `MMDLoader` and `MMDAnimationHelper` for years, handling the `.pmd`/`.pmx` model formats and `.vmd` motion files that the MikuMikuDance ecosystem produces. Reze Studio appears to build its editor interface on top of that foundation.

The bone count matters for performance. A 147-bone skeleton evaluated at 60 FPS in JavaScript — forward kinematics, interpolation, morph blending — is non-trivial work. Doing it in the browser without visible stutter signals either careful optimization or use of WebAssembly for the heavier math. The research sources do not confirm which approach Reze Studio takes.

The wider significance is directional: tooling for *MMD*, a format with a massive hobbyist community but almost no professional desktop interoperability, is moving to the open web. That lowers the barrier considerably for creators who do not want to install Windows-only software, and it opens the door to collaborative or cloud-based animation pipelines that desktop-native tools cannot easily offer.

concepts.definition: A JavaScript library that sits on top of WebGL, the browser's low-level graphics API. It provides a scene graph, camera system, lighting models, loaders for common 3D formats, and renderer backends, allowing developers to build interactive 3D applications without writing raw shader code. Maintained on GitHub under mrdoob/three.js.

MikuMikuDance is a free Japanese 3D animation program, originally built around Vocaloid characters and particularly Hatsune Miku. VMD (Vocaloid Motion Data) is its proprietary motion-capture and keyframe format, storing per-bone rotations and translations over time. The ecosystem has a large hobbyist community producing models and motion files freely shared online.

A technique in which a 3D mesh is bound to an underlying skeleton of bones arranged in a hierarchy. Moving a parent bone (say, the upper arm) propagates the transform down to children (forearm, hand, fingers). Animators keyframe bone rotations and translations over time; the software interpolates between them to produce smooth motion.

Stored alternate positions for mesh vertices, typically used for facial expressions or secondary shape changes. The renderer blends between the default shape and a target shape by a 0–1 weight, allowing subtle deformations that skeletal animation alone handles poorly — lip sync, brow raises, cheek puffs.

A browser API that exposes GPU-accelerated 3D graphics to JavaScript, based on OpenGL ES. It allows the browser to offload rendering work to the graphics card rather than the CPU. Libraries like Three.js exist largely to abstract its verbose, stateful API into something usable.

repos.summary: The Three.js library, authored primarily by Ricardo Cabello (mrdoob), is the most widely used JavaScript 3D library on the web. It provides renderers, scene graph management, geometry primitives, material systems, and loaders for formats including GLTF, OBJ, FBX, and MMD. Projects ranging from data visualizations to full games and creative tools are built on it.
